summary: We are testing whether NSGA-II (an evolutionary multi-objective optimizer) finds better throughput-vs-latency tradeoffs than random sampling when tuning LLM inference serving configurations in BLIS, using 500 evaluations (~50-125 seconds total compute). Three arms compare NSGA-II, uniform random, and Latin Hypercube Sampling to isolate whether selection pressure (not just better coverage) drives improvement.
key_points: Primary metric: hypervolume of the Pareto front over two objectives (maximize throughput req/s, minimize P99 TTFT ms) — NSGA-II predicted to consistently beat random's hypervolume at equal 500-evaluation budget.

Three arms: NSGA-II (pop=50, 10 generations) as h-main, uniform random as negative control, and Latin Hypercube Sampling as robustness check to separate 'better coverage' from 'selection pressure' as the active ingredient.

Confirmation criteria: NSGA-II hypervolume > LHS > random; refutation signals include >20% of random samples being non-dominated (space is 'easy'), or NSGA-II hypervolume plateauing by generation 1-2 (space too small for selection to matter).

Constraints are well-specified (TP*replicas≤8, conditional routing/scorer params, prefill<scheduled tokens) — all three implementations must enforce these, making constraint-handling code shared and reducing confounds.

Risk: the discrete/categorical nature of BLIS's ~294K-config space may blunt LHS stratification and NSGA-II crossover operators; diagnostic checks (generation-over-generation hypervolume, fraction of pruned offspring) are built into the design to detect this.
